podcast.title: Emigration to the UK (June 1961)
podcast.body: Desperate to leave South Africa, Lubawitz seized an opportunity in June 1961 when he was still a Commonwealth citizen, just before South Africa lost its Commonwealth membership and its citizens' automatic right to immigrate to the UK. He was part of a year's grace period for this change. "Manfrid desperately wanted to get out of South Africa, and he took his chance in June 1961, at the last point at which he was a Commonwealth citizen."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Birth Name and Origin
podcast.body: Born Manfred Lubawitz in South Africa, he came from a wealthy family but was strongly opposed to the system of apartheid and considered himself anti-racist. He was a lover of jazz music, especially progressive musicians like Ornette Coleman, Charles Mingus, and John Coltrane. "Manfrid man, the human being, as opposed to Manfrid man the group, was born Manfrid Lubawitz in South Africa, and while he was from a wealthy family, he was very opposed to the vicious South African system of apartheid, and considered himself strongly anti-racist."

podcast.title: Early Jazz Career
podcast.body: Lubawitz became a very competent jazz pianist, playing with musicians like Hugh Massacala. This was at a time when fraternisation between people of different races was strongly frowned upon in South Africa. "He soon became a very competent jazz pianist, playing with musicians like Hugh Massacala, at the time when that kind of fraternisation between people of different races was very much frowned upon in South Africa."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early London Life and Pseudonym
podcast.body: After moving to England, he started playing jazz keyboards and giving piano lessons. He also earned money by writing record reviews, for which he adopted the pseudonym "Manfred Man" (initially spelled with a 't' on the end, which he later dropped), taken from jazz drummer Shelley Man. "For those reviews, rather than credit himself as Manfred Lubawitz, he decided to use a pseudonym taken from the jazz drummer Shelley Man, and he became Manfred Man, spelled with a salinity on the end, which he later dropped."

podcast.title: Temporary Job with Graham Bond
podcast.body: Needing gigs, Manfred took a job playing with a holiday camp band as a substitute keyboard player. Graham Bond, leader of the Graham Bond Organisation, was playing Hammond organ in the same band but only wanted to play a few days a week, allowing Manfred to fill in. "Man was rather desperate for gates, and he ended up taking a job playing with a band that had put the insolidate camp. Graham Bond, who we've seen in several previous episodes as the leader of the Graham Bond organisation, was at that time playing Hammondog in there, but only wanted to play a few days a week."
